latent_mechanisms.display_name: Excess heat load above dissipation capacity
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Net endogenous or environmental heat gain overwhelms evaporative, conductive, convective, and circulatory heat dissipation, producing pathologic core hyperthermia.
Hypothalamic, autonomic, sweating, skin blood flow, behavioral, medication, or age-related failure to increase heat loss under high heat load.
Cellular protein denaturation, membrane injury, mitochondrial dysfunction, and heat-shock response failure from sustained high tissue temperature.
Gut barrier injury, endotoxemia, cytokine storm, complement activation, and innate immune activation create a sepsis-like syndrome without requiring infection.
Volume depletion, peripheral vasodilation, capillary leak, myocardial stress, and acidosis lower effective perfusion and drive lactate, shock, renal, hepatic, CNS, and gut injury.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Thermal and exertional skeletal muscle breakdown
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Exertion, heat cytotoxicity, ATP depletion, ischemia, and electrolyte shifts injure skeletal muscle, releasing CK, myoglobin, potassium, phosphate, and inflammatory mediators.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Renal pigment nephropathy and hypoperfusion injury
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Myoglobin nephrotoxicity, renal vasoconstriction, hypovolemia, shock, acidosis, and tubular injury produce AKI and oliguria/anuria.
Heat, cytokines, tissue factor exposure, platelet activation/consumption, fibrinolysis, and microvascular thrombosis produce heatstroke-induced coagulopathy that can progress to DIC and bleeding.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: CNS thermal, hypoxic, and edematous injury
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Direct heat toxicity, hypoperfusion, endothelial injury, cerebral edema, and sometimes microthrombosis or hemorrhage produce encephalopathy, seizure, coma, and delayed neurologic injury.
Thermal injury, hypoxic hepatitis, microthrombosis, cytokines, gut endotoxemia, and mitochondrial failure cause marked transaminitis and, in a minority, acute liver failure.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Hot environment increases external heat gain and reduces the gradient for heat loss.
High-intensity exertion rapidly generates endogenous heat.
Advanced age, medications, dehydration, alcohol, clothing/PPE, humidity, or poor acclimatization impair heat loss.
Longer duration of uncontrolled hyperthermia increases thermal cytotoxicity.
Effective evaporative, immersion, conductive, or cold-fluid cooling rapidly reduces net heat load.
Core temperature rises when heat load exceeds heat dissipation.
Failure of sweating, cutaneous blood flow, behavior, or external cooling sustains hyperthermia.
Cell injury and gut barrier disruption amplify cytokine and endotoxin-mediated injury.
Neurons and cerebellar Purkinje cells are heat sensitive; direct thermal injury can occur early.
Heat and ATP depletion directly injure skeletal muscle, especially during exertional heat stroke.
Cytokine and endotoxin signaling create vasodilation, capillary leak, and shock-like physiology.
Vasodilation, volume depletion, and myocardial dysfunction lower perfusion pressure.
Hypoperfusion and hypermetabolism increase anaerobic metabolism and lactate.
Sepsis-like vasoplegia and volume depletion drive shock risk.
Skeletal muscle injury releases CK, often peaking after presentation and sometimes with a second peak.
Myoglobin rises early with rhabdomyolysis and can precede or exceed CK kinetics.
Severe muscle breakdown produces clinically consequential rhabdomyolysis.
Muscle lysis and AKI can raise serum potassium.
Pigment nephropathy and hypoperfusion produce AKI.
AKI and shock often present with oliguria or anuria.
Rhabdomyolysis and hypoperfusion create high AKI risk.
Platelet activation and consumption lower platelet count in heatstroke-induced coagulopathy and DIC.
Coagulation factor consumption and hepatic injury prolong PT/INR.
Fibrin formation and breakdown raise D-dimer.
Severe heatstroke coagulopathy can progress to overt DIC.
CNS dysfunction is central to heat stroke and ranges from confusion to coma.
Severe CNS injury lowers GCS.
CNS heat injury can become structural brain injury with edema, hemorrhage, or delayed neurologic sequelae.
Heat, hypoxia, endothelial injury, and cytotoxic edema can cause rapid cerebral edema.
Thermal/hypoxic hepatic injury raises AST, though AST may also reflect muscle injury.
Hepatocellular necrosis raises ALT.
Severe acute liver injury and cholestasis raise bilirubin later than transaminases.
Marked hepatocellular necrosis plus coagulopathy can progress to acute liver failure.
Heat stress, tachycardia, shock, and acidosis can injure myocardium.
Capillary leak, systemic inflammation, transfusion, and shock can progress to lung injury and ARDS.
Severe persistent coma, cerebral edema, seizure, or structural brain injury sharply worsens survival.
Shock and tissue hypoperfusion drive multi-organ failure and death.
Acute liver failure after heat stroke has unpredictable but substantial mortality.

axes.shape_free_text: Recent exposure to high ambient heat, radiant heat, enclosed hot environment, heat wave, or high humidity; can be absent in exertional cases under only moderate ambient temperatures.
Ambient temperature preceding collapse; high values support heat exposure but heat stroke can occur at moderate temperatures with exertion, humidity, clothing, or impaired heat loss.
Environmental humidity limiting evaporative heat loss; particularly important when exertion or protective clothing is present.
Recent heavy exercise, training run, labor, military drill, or other high metabolic heat production before collapse.

Reduced ability to dissipate heat from dehydration, high humidity, heavy clothing/PPE, alcohol or sedative exposure, anticholinergic/sympathomimetic/antipsychotic drugs, older age, poor acclimatization, skin disease, or autonomic dysfunction.
Clinical volume depletion from sweating, poor intake, gastroenteritis, limited hydration, heat exposure, or osmotic/diuretic losses.
Core temperature usually above 40 C before cooling; measured arrival temperature may be lower after prehospital cooling.
Time from collapse or recognition to effective cooling that meaningfully lowers core temperature; prolonged delay increases CNS and organ injury.
Adequacy of active cooling such as cold-water immersion, evaporative cooling, ice packs, chilled fluids, or intravascular/extracorporeal cooling.
Confusion, delirium, agitation, stupor, seizure, or coma; CNS dysfunction is required clinically but final diagnostic labels should not be used as ordinary ranking evidence.
GCS falls with severe heat-stroke encephalopathy or structural CNS injury.
Seizures can occur with severe CNS heat injury, cerebral edema, electrolyte derangement, or hypoxia.
Tachycardia from hyperthermia, exertion, volume depletion, shock, pain, and catecholamines; extreme tachycardia raises cardiac injury risk.
Tachypnea from hyperthermia, metabolic acidosis, shock, ARDS, or CNS injury.
Often initially preserved unless ARDS, aspiration, pulmonary edema, shock, or CNS respiratory failure develops; falls in severe MODS.
Falls with ARDS, aspiration, pulmonary edema, or ventilator-associated oxygenation failure.
Can be low from volume depletion, vasodilation, capillary leak, myocardial injury, and acidosis; may normalize after fluids or vasopressors.
Rises with shock, hypermetabolism, hypoperfusion, seizures/exertion, hepatic dysfunction, and mitochondrial stress.
May fall with lactic acidosis, renal failure, shock, and rhabdomyolysis; respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation can mask metabolic acidosis early.
Falls with lactic acidosis and renal failure; may improve with perfusion, ventilation, renal support, and correction of hyperthermia.
Can rise with rhabdomyolysis, acidosis, and AKI; may fall after resuscitation, intracellular shift, dialysis, or renal recovery.
Falls with shock, pigment nephropathy, renal vasoconstriction, and ATN; anuria is a severe AKI marker.
Rises with AKI from pigment nephropathy, hypoperfusion, dehydration, and renal tubular injury.
Rises with AKI, dehydration, catabolism, GI bleeding, and high protein breakdown.
Often rises after presentation and may exceed 10,000-100,000 U/L in severe exertional cases; delayed or bimodal peaks can occur.
Rises early with muscle breakdown; high values are nephrotoxic and may precede CK peak.
Rises from hepatic necrosis and muscle injury; values can reach thousands when ALF or severe rhabdomyolysis develops.
Rises with hepatocellular necrosis; extreme ALT elevation supports acute hepatic injury over isolated muscle source.
Usually later and variable; rises with severe acute liver failure, cholestasis, hemolysis, or MODS.
Rises with heatstroke-induced coagulopathy, DIC, and acute liver failure; can become extreme in transplant-level ALF.
May prolong with DIC, factor consumption, liver failure, or anticoagulant exposure.
May be normal early; falls with heatstroke-induced coagulopathy, DIC, platelet activation/consumption, dilution, bleeding, or hemolytic microangiopathy.
Can be normal/high early from acute-phase response and low when consumptive coagulopathy or hyperfibrinolysis dominates.
Rises with fibrin formation/breakdown, heatstroke-induced coagulopathy, DIC, thrombosis, and inflammation.
May be hemoconcentrated early from dehydration, then fall from bleeding, hemolysis, dilution, DIC, or microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
May rise with heat-related myocardial injury, demand ischemia, shock, tachycardia, electrolyte derangement, or myocarditis-like injury.
Hazard of clinically consequential CNS injury: persistent coma, cerebral edema, seizures, hemorrhage, ischemic/cytotoxic injury, or long-term neurologic deficit.
Hazard of cytotoxic/vasogenic cerebral edema, mass effect, or herniation physiology after severe heat stroke.
Hazard that muscle injury becomes clinically consequential rhabdomyolysis with high CK/myoglobin, electrolyte derangement, pain/weakness, or pigment AKI.
Hazard of AKI from rhabdomyolysis, hypovolemia, shock, and tubular injury; may require RRT in severe cases.
Hazard of heatstroke-associated acute liver failure with severe coagulopathy, encephalopathy attribution challenge, hyperbilirubinemia, and transplant consideration.
Hazard that heatstroke-induced coagulopathy progresses to overt DIC with thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, bleeding, microthrombosis, or MAHA.
Hazard of ARDS or severe acute lung injury from systemic inflammation, shock, aspiration, transfusion, or volume overload.
Hazard of shock requiring vasopressors or causing tissue hypoperfusion.
Hazard of myocardial injury from hyperthermia, tachycardia, shock, acidosis, electrolyte derangement, or demand ischemia.
Hazard of ventricular arrhythmia or arrest from hyperkalemia, acidosis, myocardial injury, hyperthermia, or catecholamine exposure.
Hazard of clinically significant bleeding from DIC, liver failure, thrombocytopenia, fibrinogen depletion, or invasive support.
Hazard of needing invasive ventilation for airway protection, coma, respiratory failure, ARDS, or shock.
Feasibility of immediate cold-water immersion or equivalent high-rate active cooling before transport or in the emergency department.
Need for intubation or protected airway because of coma, agitation preventing cooling, seizure, aspiration risk, hypoxemia, or shock.
Need for intermittent hemodialysis or CRRT because of anuria/oliguria, severe AKI, hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload, or severe myoglobin burden.
Need for urgent transplant-center discussion because of worsening heatstroke-associated ALF, progressive INR/bilirubin, persistent organ failure, or failure to improve with supportive care.
Risk that aggressive fluids or blood products worsen pulmonary edema, ARDS, heart failure, or renal failure.
Active bleeding or urgent invasive procedure context that makes platelet, plasma, cryoprecipitate, or fibrinogen support more consequential.
Lifespan outcome hazard emerging from persistent hyperthermia, delayed cooling, CNS injury, shock, rhabdomyolysis/AKI, ALF, DIC, ARDS, arrhythmia, and failure of organ support.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Rising core temperature directly worsens heat-stroke encephalopathy.
Magnitude and duration of hyperthermia drive CNS injury.
Delayed cooling is a major modifiable survival determinant.
Effective active cooling rapidly lowers body temperature.
Rhabdomyolysis contributes to pigment nephropathy and AKI.
Myoglobin is directly nephrotoxic in rhabdomyolysis.
Poor perfusion raises lactate.
Lactate reflects tissue hypoperfusion and severity of shock-like physiology.
Hypoperfusion and shock contribute to heatstroke-associated hepatic necrosis and ALF.
Shock and renal hypoperfusion amplify pigment nephropathy.
Hyperkalemia from rhabdomyolysis or AKI can trigger malignant arrhythmia.
Acidosis increases arrhythmia risk and reduces catecholamine responsiveness.
Severe thrombocytopenia increases bleeding risk.
Prolonged PT/INR from DIC or ALF increases bleeding risk.
DIC can produce oozing, intracranial bleeding, GI bleeding, and procedure-site bleeding.
DIC worsens bleeding, microthrombosis, organ failure, and survival.
Progressive ALF, coagulopathy, and multi-organ failure increase mortality.
Severe AKI reflects MODS and can cause hyperkalemia, acidosis, and volume complications.
Cerebral edema and herniation physiology can be fatal.
Hypoxemia and respiratory failure raise ventilation need.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cooling remains necessary, but established CNS/organ injury is less reversible after long delay.
Cold-water immersion or an equivalent high-rate method lowers temperature faster than low-intensity surface cooling.

side_effects.interpretation: Rewarming/afterdrop and shivering management require electrolyte monitoring rather than antipyretic-style management.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapidly reduces core hyperthermia and the heat-load mechanism; effect is greatest before irreversible CNS and organ injury accumulates.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: ARDS, myocardial dysfunction, or renal failure limits ongoing fluid loading.
Volume depletion is a major reversible contributor to shock and AKI.

side_effects.interpretation: Large volumes can worsen pulmonary edema or ARDS, especially after capillary leak and AKI develop.
Fluid choice and water balance can shift sodium; monitor serial electrolytes.

treatments.context_specific_role: Restores perfusion and renal flow while active cooling controls the upstream heat load.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Catecholamines can worsen tachyarrhythmia risk in hyperkalemia, acidosis, or myocardial injury.

side_effects.interpretation: Catecholamine exposure can increase arrhythmia risk when hyperkalemia or myocardial injury is present.

treatments.context_specific_role: Maintains organ perfusion when fluids and cooling are insufficient to restore MAP.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Deep coma, seizure, agitation preventing cooling, or aspiration risk increases benefit of protected airway.
In ARDS, lung-protective ventilation and oxygenation support become the key direct mechanism.

side_effects.interpretation: Sedation and positive pressure ventilation can reduce venous return and MAP.
Ventilator-associated lung injury risk if lung-protective strategy is not used.

treatments.context_specific_role: Protects airway and oxygenation during coma, seizure, shock, ARDS, or agitation that interferes with cooling.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Anuria, severe hyperkalemia, acidosis, or volume overload increases immediate benefit.
CRRT is often better tolerated than intermittent dialysis in shock.

side_effects.interpretation: Ultrafiltration or intermittent dialysis can worsen hypotension.
Anticoagulation and catheter placement can add bleeding risk in coagulopathy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Controls life-threatening electrolyte, acid-base, and volume consequences of rhabdomyolysis-associated AKI while heat and perfusion mechanisms recover.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Platelets, plasma, cryoprecipitate, or fibrinogen replacement are most consequential when bleeding or urgent procedure risk exists.
Plasma and cryoprecipitate can worsen volume overload or lung injury.

side_effects.interpretation: Blood products can contribute to TACO or worsen ARDS.
Transfusion-related lung injury or volume overload can worsen respiratory failure.

treatments.context_specific_role: Temporarily corrects consumptive coagulopathy and bleeding risk while cooling, perfusion, and organ support address the upstream heat-stroke injury.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Progressive ALF with coagulopathy and organ failure makes early transplant-center discussion more consequential.
Coagulopathy changes procedural and transfusion risks around invasive liver support or transplant.

side_effects.interpretation: Procedures, invasive monitoring, plasma exchange, or transplant surgery interact with heatstroke coagulopathy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Bundles NAC-style hepatoprotective support, glucose/electrolyte/ICP/coagulation monitoring, and early transplant-center discussion for progressive ALF; actual transplant is a rescue intervention when recovery fails.

lt_40.trajectory_modulation: More likely exertional phenotype with rhabdomyolysis and high CK when strenuous activity is present.

ge_65.trajectory_modulation: Higher classic heat-stroke susceptibility, delayed recognition, CNS injury, cardiovascular strain, and mortality.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Exertional heat stroke has greater skeletal muscle heat production and rhabdomyolysis burden.
Exertional heat stroke is strongly coupled to rhabdomyolysis.
Heat and humidity reduce heat-loss reserve and increase sustained hyperthermia.
Sustained environmental heat exposure increases duration of thermal injury.
Dehydration worsens pigment nephropathy and renal hypoperfusion.

present.trajectory_modulation: Reduced behavioral response, sweating or autonomic heat loss, and delayed discovery can increase CNS injury and mortality.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Sedation/intoxication can compound heat-stroke encephalopathy and delay rescue.
Impaired awareness or being found down can delay effective cooling.
Reduced heat loss or higher metabolic cost increases thermoregulatory failure.

present.trajectory_modulation: This is not a disease-cause prior alone; it reshapes severity after heat stroke starts.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Longer uncontrolled hyperthermia increases CNS injury.
Predisposition can amplify or prolong exertional rhabdomyolysis.
Higher muscle breakdown increases pigment nephropathy risk.
Lower organ reserve worsens shock, AKI, arrhythmia, and ALF tolerance.
Cardiorenal disease limits aggressive fluids and blood products.

supportive_care: Immediate removal from heat source, cessation of exertion, and continuous core-temperature monitoring with rectal, bladder, or esophageal probe when feasible.

Serial neurologic checks with seizure treatment, glucose/electrolyte correction, and neuroimaging only when persistent coma, focal signs, edema concern, trauma, or alternative diagnosis needs evaluation.

Frequent labs during the first 24-72 hours: CK, myoglobin when available, creatinine/BUN, potassium, bicarbonate, lactate, AST/ALT, bilirubin, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, CBC, urinalysis, and urine output.
Avoid antipyretics as a causal therapy for heat stroke; hyperthermia is not driven by a pyrogenic hypothalamic set-point.
Treat hyperkalemia, acidosis, hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia, and other electrolyte derangements with standard ICU protocols.

Rhabdomyolysis care: perfusion restoration, urine-output monitoring, avoidance of nephrotoxins, and renal replacement therapy when indicated by kidney failure, electrolytes, acidosis, or volume status.
DIC/coagulopathy care: trend platelets, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, bleeding/thrombosis; give blood products according to bleeding/procedure need rather than as isolated numeric correction.

ALF care: early hepatology and transplant-center discussion for progressive INR, bilirubin, transaminases, encephalopathy attribution concern, hypoglycemia, acidosis, or worsening multi-organ failure.
Respiratory support with aspiration precautions, lung-protective ventilation if intubated, and ARDS/volume-overload monitoring after fluids or transfusion.
After recovery, evaluate return-to-activity risk, medication contributors, acclimatization, hydration strategy, and recurrent/bimodal rhabdomyolysis susceptibility when clinically suggested.
